highlights.text: a single sound root whose core meaning is appearing, emerging, coming into view
Rising (of the sun): طَلَعَتِ الشَّمْسُ, "the sun rose"
al-ṭalʿ is the date-palm's flowering sheath, enclosing the white blossom (kāfūr)
أَطْلَعْتُكَ عَلَى الْأَمْرِ, "I informed you of the matter" (iṭlāʿ)
with a verse of Aws [ibn Ḥajar] describing such a bow
centers on the sense of overturning, scattering, and turning something inside-out or upside-down
baʿthara al-shayʾ = he scattered/dispersed a thing
"they baʿtharū / baḥtharū their belongings" means they overturned them
the everyday expression "I baʿthara-ed my trough," meaning I demolished it
al-Farrāʾ explains this as the graves' interior contents (gold, silver) being brought out, followed by the dead themselves coming out
Al-Zajjāj glosses the same verse as: its soil was overturned and the dead within it were raised up
Abū ʿUbayda glosses this as "stirred up and brought out" (uthīra wa-ukhrija)
one root whose senses all trace back to a single core: **the chest / breast** (al-ṣadr)
الْبَلَد is "the chest [central part] of the villages" — i.e. an inhabited place
Ibn Fāris cites Dhū al-Rumma's line of a camel casting her chest down in a silent place
highlights.note: Dhū al-Rumma, Umayyad; no earlier witness

highlights.text: He supports the extension with Ibn al-Riqāʿ's verse on decay enveloping "its abilād" (its tracts)
highlights.note: Ibn al-Riqāʿ, Umayyad; no earlier witness

highlights.text: burūj (sing. burj): palaces, lofty towers
From this the "towers" of the sky are named, because of the stations assigned particularly to them
Hence tabarrajat al-marʾa: the woman made herself like such a garment by putting her beauties on show
For the celestial reading, Zuhayr: whoever dreads the causes of death is overtaken by them even if he reaches the means of heaven by a ladder
one single meaning, from which he says every use follows without exception: a thing's becoming visible, coming out into the open
to emerge, come into view. بَرَزَ الشَّيْءُ = the thing came out
open, wide ground. Named so, he says, because such ground lies exposed to view
cited from a line of Labīd contrasting "the speaking mubarwaz" with "the sealed."
a single root-idea — "overcoming, subduing" (al-ghalabah wal-qahr)
dahr is named from this sense because it comes upon everything and overcomes it
as shown in verses he quotes (by ʿAmr al-Ḍubaʿī and an unnamed poet), which personify time as an archer that strikes without being struck back and that robs without restoring
The Prophet's statement corrects this: the true agent behind these events is God, not dahr
الدَّرْء (al-darʾ) is a leaning or inclining toward one of the two sides
دَرَأْتُ عنه means "I repelled from his side."
"they repel the evil deed with the good one" (13:22)
Al-Rāghib also cites a ḥadīth, "repel the ḥudūd by means of doubts," which he reads as pointing to seeking some means by which the penalty can be pushed away.
one sound root whose single idea is **an opening-up in something**
الفُرْجَة (furja) is the gap in a wall or in anything else — a cleft or split. Verb: فَرَجْتُهُ / فَرَّجْتُهُ, "I opened it."
Cited from Imruʾ al-Qays: the mare "has a tail like a bride's train, with which she closes her farj from behind."
three separate root meanings: (1) laying bare or uncovering something, (2) a kind of animal, and (3) lightness and flightiness
The verb is فرّ يفرّ, "to flee". Al-mafarr is both the verbal noun and the place one flees to.
A proverb says of a good horse, "the sight of him is his teeth-examination" (عينه فِراره)
two sound, independent roots: (1) remaining or lasting, and (2) a colour — that of dust
غَبَرَ (ghabara) = "he/it remained."
غُبَار (ghubār, dust) is named from its غُبْرَة (ghubra), i.e. its colour
Shāhid from Ṭarafa: "I saw that the Banū Ghabrāʾ do not disown me
attributed to Ibn Muqbil (or another): "If Sulaymā asks after me, tell her — a remnant of his malady is in him
a single sound root carrying two joined ideas: emptiness (khuluww) and falling/dropping (suqūṭ)
al-hawā (desire, the inclination of the soul)
He cites Q 14:43, "their hearts are hawāʾ" (void, comprehending nothing)
al-hāwiya = any abyss; al-huwwa = a deep pit
a line of Zuhayr describing an ostrich whose breast is hollow (hawāʾ)
Zuhayr for descent (like a well-bucket dropping)
a single root (aṣl wāḥid) whose meaning is covering and concealment
al-janna is also an orchard, because trees conceal with their leaves
al-jinna is madness, because it covers the mind; al-majanna also means madness
al-mijann is a shield, and any weapon one is concealed behind is a junna
citing Zuhayr's verse comparing his weeping eyes to the buckets of a water-drawing camel
Three distinct roots share these letters: (1) watching-over/safekeeping, (2) vegetation/pasture, (3) a bodily organ (the kidney), later borrowed metaphorically
kalaʾahu Allāh — God preserved/protected him
glossed as: no one shields you from Him; connected to "watching"
a line of poetry about keeping watch with a couched camel's eye
a single sound root whose core sense is joining one thing to another
الكِتاب (a written document) and الكِتابة (writing) — since writing joins letters and words together
Here الكِتاب means an imposed obligation, as in {kutiba ʿalaykum al-ṣiyām} — "fasting is prescribed for you" (Q 2:183)
al-Jaʿdī's line: "the kitāb of God has driven me out from you — can I ward off from God what He has done?"
كِتاب can mean a verdict, as in the Prophet's saying that he would judge "by the kitāb of God," glossed as "by His ruling."
المُكاتَب is a slave with whom his master makes a kātaba agreement to buy his own freedom
this root's two clusters of meaning: "play" and "saliva/drool."
اللَعِب / اللَّعْب (al-laʿib / al-laʿb): "play, playing" — the two forms are equivalent
Abū Barāʾ was titled ملاعب الأسِنّة (Mulāʿib al-Asinna, "player with the spear-heads"), which Labīd altered to ملاعب الرماح (Mulāʿib al-Rimāḥ, "player with the lances") to fit his rhyme
a sound root with two meanings: keeping close and staying fixed, and purity and excellence
Lubb of anything is its pure part, what is picked out of it. For this reason, he says, the intellect is called lubb.
A verse likens a woman "gleaming of neck and upper breast" to a gazelle that such sand has brought into view.
al-layl is what follows the day, beginning at sunset
the unit-noun is laylah ("a night")
Parallel adjectives for a dark/deep night: alyal, lāʾil, mulayyal (this last possibly meaning "abundant [in nights]," as if intensified), with a shāhid from ʿAmr b. Shaʾs
a single sound root whose core sense is the correspondence or matching of one thing to another
هَذَا مِثْلُ هَذَا means "this is the counterpart (naẓīr) of this."
because a proverb is cited allusively to stand in place of something it resembles in meaning
glossing al-mathulāt as "the punishments that deter from the like of what caused them."
a single core idea: the going-out of breath or breeze (however it occurs, from wind or anything else)
تَنَفُّس (tanaffus) is breathing — breath leaving the body's inner cavity
A prized thing is نَفِيس (nafīs): it has نَفْس (worth/consequence) and is competed for; hence تَنَافُس (rivalry)
Ibn Fāris cites two ḥadīths for this sense: "Do not curse the wind, for it is from the nafas of the Merciful"
highlights.note: a hadith on nafas as relief

highlights.text: two sound origins: (a) the pure, noble core of a thing, and (b) turning something from one side to another
al-qalb = the heart (of a human or animal), named because it is the purest and highest thing in the body
qalabtu al-shayʾ = I overturned it; qallabtu (with intensive form) = I turned it over repeatedly by hand
most words of q-s-s concern following something up, tracking it (tatabbuʿ al-shayʾ)
one root meaning accord, coming alongside, and closeness without harshness
the elbow, so called because one rests by leaning on it
The verb ارْتَفَقَ (irtafaqa) = to prop oneself on the elbow while seated
رَفِيق (rafīq), the individual companion — one who shares a rufqa with you
precedence, priority in time or place
السَّلَف (salaf) — those who have gone before, predecessors
one underlying idea for this root — "persisting/continuing upon a thing"
A band/troop of horsemen; plurals ثُبَات (thubāt) and ثُبُون (thubūn)
a verse of ʿAmr, "our horses become bands, troops," describing a day they feared for their people
a single core idea: doubling a thing twice, or making it into two parts
الاثْنَان ("the two") is the well-known numeral from this root
Ibn Fāris ties grammatical "exception" (استثناء) to the root's core sense of doubling
explaining the name as meaning that its recitation is doubled and repeated
lines by Maʿn and al-Namir b. Tawlab using ثِنَى / ثُنْيَان for blame that is repeated
highlights.note: Maʿn, al-Namir b. Tawlab, lived into Islam

highlights.text: Ibn Fāris quotes the prophetic saying «لَا ثِنَى فِي الصَّدَقَةِ» — glossed as: ṣadaqa is not taken twice in a single year
